source: Da Costa, Parr, Sajid, Veselic, Neacsu, Friston (2020) Active inference on discrete state-spaces: a synthesis
finding: Core definition. The expected free energy G of a policy can be written two ways. Risk plus ambiguity: KL between predicted and preferred outcomes, plus expected entropy of outcomes given states. Or: negative expected information gain about hidden states, minus expected log preferred outcomes. Policy probability is a softmax of minus G.
numbers: Eq 13: G = D_KL[Q(s,A|pi)||P(s,A)] + E[H[P(o|s,A)]]. Policy posterior Q(pi)=softmax(-gamma*G). Epistemic parts named salience (states) and novelty (parameters).
quote: policy selection minimises risk and ambiguity
limits: Review and tutorial; the maths is a derivation, not an empirical test. Prior preferences P(o|C) must be supplied by the designer.
agent_relevance: S7 'pick the test that most separates hypotheses' is the epistemic term: expected information gain about hidden state. Preferences are the pragmatic term, i.e. the goal checker.

source: Da Costa, Parr, Sajid, Veselic, Neacsu, Friston (2020) Active inference on discrete state-spaces: a synthesis
finding: The paper says the intrinsic (epistemic) value is the same quantity as optimal Bayesian design, active learning and Bayesian surprise in visual search. So active inference decision theory contains Lindley-style experiment selection as a special case when preferences are flat.
numbers: Section 7 links epistemic value to Bayesian design [157], active learning [158], Bayesian surprise and mutual information in salience literature [153,155].
limits: A claim of unification made by the authors. Old results (Lindley 1956, MacKay 1992) already gave the expected information gain; the novelty is adding it to reward in one objective.
agent_relevance: Confirms that for our agent the S7 discriminating-test rule is not exotic: it is classical Bayesian experimental design.

source: Da Costa, Parr, Sajid, Veselic, Neacsu, Friston (2020) Active inference on discrete state-spaces: a synthesis
finding: With discrete states the whole scheme is a few matrices: likelihood A, transitions B, preferences C, initial state D. Learning is done by Dirichlet counts on A, which adds a novelty term that rewards visiting poorly known state-outcome pairs.
numbers: Appendix C gives closed forms for ambiguity (C.1) and novelty (C.3). Novelty = expected KL between updated and prior Dirichlet A.
limits: Tractable only for small discrete models; policies are enumerated, so cost grows with number of policies.
agent_relevance: For a hypothesis set of 2 to 10 rules, an explicit table of predicted outcomes per test is the analogue of A; this is cheap to compute by code outside the model.

source: Friston, Rigoli, Ognibene, Mathys, FitzGerald, Pezzulo (2015) Active inference and epistemic value
finding: Founding paper for epistemic value in active inference. Not opened (paywalled). Described in the secondary sources as showing that minimising expected free energy gives both goal seeking and information seeking in a T-maze with a cue, with no separate exploration bonus.
numbers: Numbers not available from this session; do not cite specifics from it.
limits: Not read. Treat all claims here as second-hand via Sajid 2021 and Da Costa 2020.
agent_relevance: Do not cite exact results from this paper in the schema until it is opened.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Compares active inference with reinforcement learning on FrozenLake. Setting preferences over outcomes plays the role of reward. With flat preferences (null model), the agent acts to resolve uncertainty only and reaches the goal about as often as the hole.
numbers: Table 1, 200 trials x 500 episodes. Deterministic: AIF 99.88 [99.64,100]; Bayesian RL 99.76; Q-learning 97.79 or 80.44. Null AIF 50.03 [49.70,50.35]. Null AIF ended in goal 44.0% of the time.
quote: if one removes uncertainty -- in the form of epistemic value -- we are left with pragmatic value
limits: One toy grid world. Authors say FrozenLake is not representative of all discrete environments.
agent_relevance: Shows the pure epistemic objective does not pursue the goal. For S7, information gain must be tied to a goal check (the pragmatic term), or the agent probes forever.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: In a stochastic FrozenLake, the active inference agent scored far above Q-learning and Bayesian model-based RL. Authors credit the epistemic term and belief-based planning.
limits: Authors designed both the task and the active inference model; the preference vector was strongly set. Bayesian RL had no explicit information bonus, so this is not a clean test of epistemic value alone.
agent_relevance: A caution: reported gains may come from setup choices. Do not assume that adding an information term alone gives the gain.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: When only a negative preference (avoid the hole) is given, belief-based agents avoid both candidate hole locations and only stop at the time limit. The result depends entirely on the generative model, not on the principle.
numbers: Table 2 second row: all three agents learn the same circular behaviour; no goal-seeking.
limits: Authors note behaviour follows from the form of the generative model, so the model must be right.
agent_relevance: Failure mode for S7: an under-specified hypothesis set makes the agent avoid everything. Keep the hypothesis set and the goal explicit.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Epistemic value and learning interact: with Dirichlet-learned likelihood and preferences, the agent first visits every location (novelty), then settles to exploit once uncertainty falls. Explore turns into exploit without a switch.
numbers: Simulated 10 times; after learning, the agent hides in holes it has learned to prefer (Fig 6). Exploration stops as uncertainty falls.
limits: Simulation only, 10 runs; preferences learned can be arbitrary (agent learned to prefer holes).
agent_relevance: Supports a stopping rule: when expected information gain of the best test falls below a threshold, go to S8 verify. This is a natural exit from S7.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2021) Whence the expected free energy?
finding: Key critique. The EFE is not 'the variational free energy in the future'. A straightforward extension of the free energy to the future (the FEF) actively discourages exploration, because its epistemic term has the opposite sign. Exploration is added by the EFE definition, not derived from free energy minimisation.
numbers: Section 4: epistemic value is positive in the FEF and negative in the EFE. EFE is a lower bound on expected model evidence when information gain exceeds posterior error, and an upper bound in the other case.
quote: exploration does not directly follow from free energy minimization into the future
limits: A theoretical paper with no human data. Authors say it does not question the usefulness of the EFE, only its derivation.
agent_relevance: The claim 'curiosity follows from free energy minimisation' is contested; for design, treat expected information gain as an added term we choose, not as a theorem.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Buckley (2021) Whence the expected free energy?
finding: Proposes the Free Energy of the Expected Future (FEEF): the divergence between predicted and desired futures. It contains the same epistemic term as the EFE plus a clear bound on a defined quantity. The EFE is not a valid bound under the temporal mean-field used in the usual scheme.
numbers: FEEF = KL between a veridical and a biased generative model over future observations; contains expected information gain. Appendix 12 to 13 review other derivations.
limits: Theory; the FEEF is validated only in the companion RL paper (a21).
agent_relevance: Gives an alternative objective whose epistemic part is still expected information gain, so S7 test choice is stable across variants.

source: Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2021) Understanding the origin of information-seeking exploration in probabilistic objectives for control
finding: Splits objectives into evidence objectives (reward maximising, no exploration) and divergence objectives (match expected to desired futures, give information gain). Claims divergence objectives explain probability matching in bandit tasks.
numbers: Example: with a 90% and a 10% option, utility maximisation picks the 90% one 100% of the time; people choose the 10% one about 10% of the time; the divergence objective gives that matching.
limits: Explanation of human behaviour is argued mathematically, not fitted to subject data in this paper. Probability matching also has other accounts.
agent_relevance: Note that a divergence objective deliberately samples non-best options; for answer selection (S7) this is not wanted, only for test selection.

source: Schwartenbeck et al. (2019) Computational mechanisms of curiosity and goal-directed exploration
finding: Separates two kinds of information gain: hidden-state exploration (active inference) and model-parameter exploration (active learning). They make different predictions. Tested in a simulated T-maze with a safe arm and a risky arm, 32 trials per run.
numbers: Fig 6: 1000 simulated experiments of 32 trials, true reward probability 0.5. Fig 7 task: context sets risky reward chance to 75% or 25%, and a cue reveals the context.
limits: Simulations only; no participants. Reviewers asked how robust results are to the Dirichlet prior a0 and the reward vector c; behaviour depends on both.
agent_relevance: S7 should say which uncertainty a test resolves: which hypothesis is true (state) or how the world works (parameters).

source: Schwartenbeck et al. (2019) Computational mechanisms of curiosity and goal-directed exploration
finding: Ablations show each term is needed. Without the state-information term the agent never samples the cue and sticks with the safe option. Without the parameter-learning term the agent cannot adapt to new reward statistics. Random exploration is a weaker substitute.
numbers: Fig 9 'broken active inference': agent keeps preferring the safe option although risky reward chance is constant high. Fig 5 broken active learning: precise agent never discovers the risky option is better.
limits: Qualitative simulated curves; no tabulated effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Supports having an explicit information-seeking step; absent it, an agent can lock into a safe but wrong answer.

source: Schwartenbeck et al. (2019) Computational mechanisms of curiosity and goal-directed exploration
finding: The model reproduces a reported primate result: the value of information rises with expected reward. Monkeys preferred an informative option more when both options paid more water.
numbers: Fig 13 cites Blanchard et al. 2015: preference for the informative option is stronger when both options give 315 microlitres than 75 microlitres.
limits: Cited empirical result, not re-run here; one monkey study.
agent_relevance: Suggests information-seeking should scale with stakes: spend more on discriminating tests when the answer matters more (G12 spend by difficulty).

source: Da Costa, Sajid, Parr, Friston, Smith (2023) Reward maximisation through discrete active inference
finding: Formal result: standard active inference with expected free energy gives Bellman-optimal actions only at planning horizon 1 in a POMDP, not beyond. Sophisticated inference (recursive) gives Bellman-optimal actions at any finite horizon.
numbers: Abstract: 'Bellman optimal actions for planning horizons of 1, but not beyond'; sophisticated scheme optimal on any finite horizon.
quote: can produce Bellman optimal actions for planning horizons of 1, but not beyond
limits: Proof for finite-horizon discrete MDP and POMDP with exact state estimation; says nothing about approximate or large models.
agent_relevance: Supports one-step lookahead test selection (greedy information gain) as the sound regime; deeper plans need the recursive form or search.

source: Da Costa, Sajid, Parr, Friston, Smith (2023) Reward maximisation through discrete active inference
finding: Active inference maximises reward when preferences are set as log of reward. With no epistemic term it reduces to expected reward; so RL is a special case. Authors state sophisticated inference will vastly outperform standard active inference, but is costly.
numbers: Section 6: sophisticated scheme is tractable only with pruning of low-probability branches.
limits: Equivalence needs the preferences to encode reward exactly; no empirical benchmark in this paper.
agent_relevance: Reward-style scoring and information-style scoring can be one scoring rule in code.

source: Friston, Da Costa, Hafner, Hesp, Parr (2021) Sophisticated inference
finding: Sophisticated inference rewrites the expected free energy recursively, as beliefs about beliefs. Tree search only follows branches with enough predictive probability. It can be stopped at any depth.
numbers: Eq 1.11 gives expected free energy of next action as risk plus ambiguity plus expected EFE of future beliefs. Simulations: T-maze (3 arms), 8x8 grid maze, novelty-seeking rat with 8 moves and horizon 4.
limits: Simulated demonstrations by the framework's authors; compute cost grows with depth and branching.
agent_relevance: A template for pruned multi-step test planning at S6 impasses: follow only likely outcomes.

source: Friston, Da Costa, Hafner, Hesp, Parr (2021) Sophisticated inference
finding: In the T-maze, a sophisticated agent with deep search (depth 2) reproduces the shallow agent's cue-then-reward sequence. The sequence is epistemic action (look at the cue) before pragmatic action (pick an arm).
numbers: Deep policy search of depth 2 reproduces earlier figure results; 3-arm T-maze.
limits: Toy task with one informative cue and known model.
agent_relevance: The 'look first, then commit' order is exactly S7 discriminating test before S8 verify.

source: Tschantz, Baltieri, Seth, Buckley (2019) Scaling active inference
finding: First scaled implementation: deep neural nets for the model, expected free energy with information gain, trained on continuous control. Information gain drives wider exploration than reward only or epsilon-greedy noise. Order of magnitude better sample efficiency than DDPG.
numbers: MountainCar: 100 epochs, state coverage larger than reward agent and epsilon-greedy (noise variance 0.3); inverted pendulum and hopper: strong performance in under 100 epochs vs 1500 for DDPG; 5 seeds, 95% interquartile range.
limits: Coverage shown as figure only; 5 seeds; exploitation tasks used only the extrinsic term, so epistemic value was not tested there.
agent_relevance: Evidence that information gain beats random noise for exploration; it also avoids the noisy-TV problem because it counts belief change, not raw signal.

source: Tschantz, Baltieri, Seth, Buckley (2019) Scaling active inference
finding: Cites why information gain suits exploration: it outperforms prediction error and avoids the noisy-TV problem, since unpredictable noise gives no belief change.
numbers: Text cites [63] for information gain beating prediction error; origin traced to Lindley and dynamic-programming work [64,65].
limits: Review statement, not an experiment in the paper.
agent_relevance: Use belief-change measures, not output variety, to decide a test is informative; random variation is not information.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: FEEF agent balances exploration and exploitation in one objective. Solves sparse-reward MountainCar in a single trial; matches baselines on Cup Catch; works with no reward on Ant Maze.
numbers: MountainCar: 25 episodes of at most 200 steps, optimal performance after one trial while baselines mostly fail; Ant Maze: coverage percent after 35 episodes vs random baseline; Half Cheetah run and flip vs SAC.
limits: Workshop paper (ICLR 2020 BAICS); few seeds; Cup Catch showed no gain; no statistical tests.
agent_relevance: Gain from the epistemic term appears when reward is sparse, i.e. when the checker gives no signal. Matches our no-check mode.

source: Champion, Bowman, Grzes (2023) Deconstructing deep active inference
finding: Independent re-implementation of deep active inference on the dSprites task with five EFE definitions and three action rules. Only models that maximise reward solved the task. The agent minimising EFE kept choosing one action and gathered too little data for the others.
numbers: Five EFE definitions x three action selection strategies; CKA similarity shows the reward and EFE critics differ in the last layer; EFE model confident only about action 'down'.
quote: the models able to solve the dSprites environment are the ones that maximise rewards
limits: One environment (dSprites); deep approximation, so failures may come from approximations, not the principle. Authors also report discrepancies between a published paper and its code.
agent_relevance: A failed replication-like result: the EFE objective did not beat plain reward in a deep agent. Be careful about claiming EFE selection beats simpler scoring.

source: Champion, Bowman, Grzes (2023) Deconstructing deep active inference
finding: Champion reviews and fixes the EFE used in prior deep active inference (Fountas et al. 2020) and gives an alternative with entropy terms. Reports discrepancies between that paper and its code, and DAIMC (a version with MCTS) does solve dSprites.
numbers: Equation 8 vs the authors' alternative; Appendix B lists discrepancies.
limits: Single-lab reimplementation; findings on one task.
agent_relevance: Published EFE results are fragile; do not rely on one lab's numbers.

source: de Vries et al. (2025) Expected free energy-based planning as variational inference
finding: Shows EFE planning can be cast as variational inference on a model augmented with preference and epistemic priors, with a complexity term for bounded compute. Authors admit it is conceptual: no implementation details and no simulation validation yet.
numbers: Quote of limits: results 'remain conceptual'; validation through simulations 'has yet to be performed'.
quote: validation through simulations has yet to be performed
limits: Theory only. 2025 preprint, v4.
agent_relevance: A resource-aware EFE (bounded compute) is the type of thing the budget rule G12 wants; still unproven.

source: Sajid, Tigas, Zakharov, Fountas, Friston (2021) Exploration and preference satisfaction trade-off in reward-free learning
finding: Agent that learns its own preferences with conjugate priors plus EFE planning. In stable worlds it converges on confident preferences and acts to satisfy them. Under constant volatility it keeps exploring, because preference uncertainty never falls.
numbers: FrozenLake and a 3D environment; volatility 0, 25, 50, 75, 100% (map switched every 40, 20, 10 or 1 steps); 10 seeds with 95% CI; at 100% volatility behaviour returns toward exploration.
limits: Toy and small 3D worlds; own-lab simulation.
agent_relevance: If the goal is uncertain (no check, open mode), information seeking keeps going. Needs a budget stop.

source: Hafner, Ortega, Ba, Parr, Friston, Heess (2022) Action and perception as divergence minimization
finding: Puts reward maximisation, information gain, empowerment and skill discovery on one spectrum, as divergence minimisation with a latent-variable model. Information gain is one point on it.
numbers: Theoretical map; abstract lists representation learning, information gain, empowerment, skill discovery.
limits: Abstract and figure read only; I did not check its experiments.
agent_relevance: Evidence that 'expected information gain' is one choice among several objectives, not unique to active inference.

source: Ueltzhoeffer (2018) Deep active inference
finding: Early neural implementation of active inference. Notes that optimising the bound for active agents needs the true dynamics of the world, which the agent does not have, so a learned model stands in.
numbers: Published in Biological Cybernetics 2018 (doi 10.1007/s00422-018-0785-7); I read only the introduction.
limits: Only the introduction read; results not examined here.
agent_relevance: Shows the first step to scale: replace the exact model with a learned one. For an LLM, the model is the LLM plus code checks.

source: Friston, Parr, de Vries (2017) The graphical brain: belief propagation and active inference (cited via Da Costa 2020)
finding: Cited as the origin of the message-passing form of the scheme. Not opened.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: None without opening.
